reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .306, 99th percentile, and the contact quality underneath it is what makes the .282 projection feel conservative rather than hopeful. At 92.9 mph average exit velocity and 52.2% hard-hit rate, he's doing elite contact damage, and the 30.3 ft/s sprint speed converts a portion of that damage that would retire anyone else. The one friction point is a 33.0% chase rate, which suppresses his walk opportunities and is the reason the OBP projection stays at .351 despite the raw contact ability; if that rate tightens even modestly, the offensive profile takes a significant step up. He's already a true shortstop, a 42-steal threat in projection, and a .819 OPS hitter — the question isn't whether he's good, it's how long before the chase discipline catches up to everything else he already is.

reports.name: Cam Schlittler
reports.published_report: The chase rate tells the story here: 35.1% gets hitters expanding off the zone, and when you pair that with a 4.9% walk rate, you're looking at a pitcher who manufactures weak counts without surrendering the zone to do it. His 30.5% strikeout rate leans on that chase, not on whiff volume inside, the 27.8% Whiff% is functional, not elite, so the profile is more get-ahead-and-make-them-chase than pure swing-and-miss. The 97.8 mph fastball with 2503 rpm behind it explains why hitters can't just sit on something predictable, and a 2.93 xERA with a .267 xwOBA confirms the results aren't statistical good fortune. If the chase rate erodes, the strikeouts follow, and this becomes a contact-management story he may not win at 39.4% hard contact, but right now the command-plus-stuff combination looks legitimate.

reports.name: Max Clark
reports.peak_summary: Projection: everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 408 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact is the story here. At AAA in 2026, Clark is striking out at a 15% clip across 408 plate appearances, and that translates to an 18.3% MLB-equivalent rate while the league average sits at 22.0%. That's not a platoon bat squeezing production from a favorable zone — it's a 21-year-old center fielder who rarely gives at-bats away, walking 49 times against only 62 strikeouts while adding 21 stolen bases. The ISO at .150 at AAA translates to .13, which is below average at the MLB level, so the ceiling depends entirely on whether he adds enough pull-side pop to punish pitchers who attack him early, and if that growth stalls, you're looking at a bat-control plus speed profile that lands somewhere between a bench bat and an everyday regular.

reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: The .422 xwOBA tells you almost everything: Soto is making elite contact quality, chasing only 19.8% of pitches while walking at 17.5%, and the combination produces an expected profile that the .948 OPS projection roughly tracks. reports.name: Shane McClanahan
reports.published_report: The ERA from his last healthy season made McClanahan look like a budding ace, but the Statcast profile from his most recent sample tells a more complicated story. His xERA sits at 4.16 with a 22.2% strikeout rate, both right at the middle of the league, which means the 3.35 ERA projection is leaning hard on contact management and a whiff-and-chase combination that has some real teeth: 27.0% whiff rate, 32.0% chase rate, both above average. The profile holds if he can keep limiting barrels, where his 8.8% barrel rate and 39.7% hard-hit rate suggest some exposure, and if his Tommy John recovery delivers a fastball that actually plays at 95.6 mph rather than just registering it. If the stuff doesn't sharpen, what's left is a rotation arm who lives on the margins of hitter mistakes.

reports.name: Cooper Pratt
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 261 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the thing. At 21, Pratt is drawing 34 walks against just 37 strikeouts across 261 AAA plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his BB% at 10.5 and his K% at 18.2, both comfortably on the right side of the league line. The power translation is the catch: his ISO comes out to .131 in MLB terms, meaningfully below where big-league averages sit, and the .241 AVG riding a .264 BABIP at AAA suggests the hit tool isn't doing extra lifting. If the discipline holds at the next level and he holds shortstop, he's a bench piece with a path to platoon value; if the BABIP normalizes down and the gap power never firms up, depth is the honest ceiling.

reports.published_report: The WHIP is 1.0 across AAA & AA, and that's the most honest thing in this profile. Wei-En Lin is limiting baserunners at an elite clip for a 20-year-old, and his 17 walks in 53 innings translate to a 3.2 BB/9 at the MLB level, matching what an average big-league starter allows, which means the command is functional but not a separator. The strikeouts are the catch: 54 punchouts across AAA & AA sounds fine until the MLB translation comes back at 8.0 K/9, a tick below where the average MLB pitcher lands, and the whole profile hinges on whether he can generate more whiffs against better hitters than he's seeing now. reports.name: Garrett Mitchell
reports.published_report: The contact is the whole problem. Mitchell's exit velocity sits at 92.6 mph and his barrel rate is 14.2%, both comfortably in the top twelve or thirteen percent of the league, and a 22.7% chase rate that ranks in the 90th percentile tells you the plate discipline is genuine. But a 36.8% whiff rate undercuts all of it, because pitchers who locate inside the zone can carve him up even when he won't bite outside it. The projection at .260/.349/.428 is basically what you get when elite raw contact quality gets taxed repeatedly by a 32.2% strikeout rate: a useful outfielder, not a dangerous one. Add 29.8 ft/s sprint speed and the floor is a legitimate everyday piece; if he ever trims the whiff rate, the underlying contact profile is loud enough to push him into genuine value territory.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 190 A PA.
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 239 A PA.
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.

reports.name: Tsung-Che Cheng
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 240 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the honest edge here. Thirty-two walks in 240 AAA plate appearances translates to a 10.5% walk rate against an MLB average of 8.5%, which is a real skill and the thing that keeps his profile from being merely a glove-and-speed placeholder. The speed is loud too, 10 stolen bases already this season, and the .351 OBP at AAA reflects both. Where it gets complicated is the power: a .17 ISO at AAA softens to .142 in MLB equivalent terms, right at or just below league average, which means the offensive profile leans heavily on getting on base rather than doing damage once he does. If the walk rate travels and the contact holds, 60 strikeouts in 240 PA is a tick above comfortable at the big-league level, Cheng is a viable bench bat who can play shortstop and run; if the strikeout rate creeps and the ISO doesn't grow, the floor is organizational depth.
